Richard Wright. The American novelist whose unsparing social realist works depicted Black poverty, racism, and existential alienation in mid-twentieth-century America. His groundbreaking novel Native Son became a watershed text in American literature, establishing him as a major voice articulating the psychological toll of systemic racism.

Native Son, published in 1940, tells the story of Bigger Thomas, a poor Black man in Chicago whose accidental killing of a white woman becomes the catalyst for exploring racism, desperation, and the making of a criminal. The novel was a bestseller and influential on American letters, though controversial for its unflinching depiction of Black criminality and racial violence. He published Black Boy in 1945, a powerful autobiography detailing his childhood poverty in the Jim Crow South and his journey to literacy and artistic consciousness.

Wright initially engaged with the Communist Party as offering solidarity against racism, but he later grew disenchanted and documented this journey in The God That Failed, published in 1949. In 1946 he emigrated to France, seeking escape from American racism, where he spent the final decade of his life writing and engaging with existentialist philosophy. His thinking was influenced by naturalism, existentialism, and Marxist analysis, and he synthesized these traditions with urgent attention to American racial reality. His work influenced younger contemporaries like James Baldwin and Ralph Ellison, who both admired and critically diverged from Wright's literary approach.
